utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. You may sit down. General Talic, good morning to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I can hear you in a language that I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours, my name is Andrew Cayley and I appear with my colleague Anna Richterova on behalf of the Prosecution with our case manager Denise Gustin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Cayley. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, good morning. My name is Milan Trbojevic, and I'm the co-counsel of Mr. Ackerman and also our assistant Madam Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Appearances for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. I'm Natasha Ivanovic-Fauveau representing General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any news, Madam Fauveau? For the record, about the appointment of the lead counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the lead counsel for General Talic arrived in The Hague yesterday. He met with General Talic, and everybody agreed that he would leave for Belgrade to regulate things over there and he will be joining us again after the break in the beginning of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: General Talic, in the meantime, are you happy with the situation? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Well, I will have to accept the situation and tolerate it till the end of the break, and I believe that Madam Ivanovic is doing her job very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't doubt that. But I want to make sure that you're not feeling prejudiced or unduly hampered in your defence. THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] I don't believe that I'm unduly hampered. And of course I would like to have the lead counsel present here as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, General Talic. If there are complaints in this context that you would like to make, please feel free to make them at any time. THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. And I thank you for the interest you've expressed. If I have anything, I will intervene. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, General Talic. You may sit down. Madam Fauveau, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could we go into private session for a while so that I can explain why the lead counsel is not coming before the end of the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I don't think you need to explain. I mean, I can quite understand that he -- any lawyer that is going to take such a burden -- take up such a burden as being a lead counsel in a trial which has already been going on for four months or so, I mean, has to wind up his business at least temporarily or as necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But there's also an administrative point. He hasn't been officially designated, and that is why he's not present in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know. I know that. I know that. Okay. That seems to have been settled or on the point of being settled once and for all, which would make everyone happier. And perhaps, Madam Richterova, you said you have 15 more minutes to go. You may have more, of course. Please proceed. Thank you. Mr. Begic, may I ask you to repeat the solemn declaration that you made yesterday, please. The usher will help you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Begic. And good morning to you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, before we adjourned yesterday you stated that you went to Mr. Krlic's house, you rested there for some time, you fell asleep in about 30 minutes, in your guess. You heard voices which were asking that you get out of the house. Did you go out of the house?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Outside a few neighbours were waiting for me from the checkpoint, and an officer unknown to me who came with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did they take you somewhere?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After our brief discussion, they took me by car to Tomina, where there is an outpatient clinic and where I was to receive medical assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you receive medical assistance?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Where did you go from this medical house?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before entering the emergency unit, I was briefly informed that I was to go later to the elementary school for questioning and see Gojko Saula for the questioning, which I did after the medical treatment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Before you were taken to medical treatment, you said that a few neighbours and an officer -- and an unknown officer took you out from the house. Was he a soldier or policeman?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a soldier. And I believe by rank that he was a lieutenant, because I knew the ranks. I also knew his name. But Vrucinic -- but at present, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know which army he belonged to?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a member of the 6th Krajina Brigade, a member of the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: After the medical treatment, you said that you were informed to go for interrogation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to the school. There was some 200 metres, and Dr. Majkic took me there, the one who gave me the -- assisted me medically, treated me. And I was accompanied also by two soldiers. And on the threshold -- at the threshold of the school we met Gojko Saula and Nedzo Sucur. Allegedly he was also to be questioned, but he had some work to do and he turned to Nedzo and told Nedzo to question me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Just to explain, why were you taken to the school?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that school at the time, these were the quarters of the army. It is there that they slept, they had their canteen and their offices. And this was where -- also the reception area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So you said that Nedzo was supposed to question you. Did he question you?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What were you talking about or what kind of questions did he ask you?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nedzo already before the -- worked in Tomina as an agricultural engineer and he knew us personally, us people from the village of Begici, we were close. And at the time when we were alone, we spoke of everything, how everything turned out for the worst, that it shouldn't have happened. He guaranteed me that it wasn't his soldiers who had done it. Then we passed on to the questioning concerning what really happened on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you said that "He guaranteed me that it wasn't his soldiers," does it mean that he was a commander of some soldiers? Did he tell you any information about his role?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. But one would understand from this that he had his units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So I will go on. And you stated that you started talking about what really happened. So what did he ask you?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he asked how did we arrive to the bridge, with whom, and what really happened with us. Because he wasn't supposedly present, and he didn't know what really happened and what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What did you tell him?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- well, I told him in detail from the moment I left my home to the moment when I again handed myself in to the Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And what was his reaction to your -- to your story?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he believed me completely. Then after a short time elapsed, he then called in a soldier to the room where we were sitting. The soldier Kaurin and he asked me whether I knew that man.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was this Kaurin the same person you mentioned as Nenad Kaurin who was at the bridge?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it's the same person.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Okay. You may go on.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And he asked me whether I knew this person and from where I knew that person. And as Nenad lived in Ilidza, which is rather close to the Vrhpolje Bridge, he was -- there was a difference between our ages some two years. I often met him in town, earlier in the school. And before the question -- he was at the checkpoint in the reserve police forces dress, that uniform, and I said that I knew this person from these -- on the basis of these occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did Nedzad Sucur ask you something more?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He asked me whether -- would it be possible that this person was on the bridge. And then I said, "When I arrived to the bridge, I was beaten also on my head and my eyes were closed, so that I couldn't recognise and identify that person."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Why did you answer that way?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: After this answer, what went on?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told Nenad to leave the room, and we continued the discussion as we had before the entry of the soldier. He in short described what the situation was in our village and the neighbouring villages. He told me that my mother was expelled to the village of the Muslim part of the village of Tomina, on the other side of the Sana, and that he will attempt to get me across too. And in the orders of Gojko Saula, it was forcing that I would be left in the boiler room of the elementary school, however that he will do it on his own responsibility to send me across but that I keep silent and never say what happened. And if I ever go out of Bosnia, that I then testify that it was he who really saved me, which I would do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did he take you to Tomina?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, together with two soldiers who were escorts, he took me to the house where my mother was staying together with my youngest brother, and he left me there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Before we will shortly talk about Tomina, I would like to return back to your village of Begici to the moment when on the 31st of May, the soldiers arrived to your village. You stated that after they arrived, they gathered you in your part of the hamlet, the lower part, and took you to the upper part. Apart from the gathering of people, did you see soldiers doing something else?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After we were leaving the buildings, they were setting fire to buildings, the barns, the hay stacks, and we could see that some women were bringing out certain valuables from those houses which were not set on fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you said "some women," did you know them?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Who were they?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were wives of the soldiers who were manning the checkpoint, namely the wives of our close neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you mean your Bosnian neighbours or your Serb neighbours?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now I would return to Tomina. You stated that you stayed in a house with your mother and youngest brother. How long did you stay in Tomina?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was the end of June and the beginning of July, after which we were moved to Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When in Tomina, were you able to observe what went on in surrounding areas?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In those days, while staying in Tomina, we helped the family with whom we were staying. We helped them in agricultural work. They had land close to the river. And this building was only a few hundred metres from the place we were staying. And my mother would go every day to the river bank and observe what was happening around our house.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And did you, you personally, see anything happening around your house?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly speaking, I didn't dare leave the house, particularly not in daytime. I could see some things happening from the terrace and I could look directly towards our house. We, however, couldn't recognise the people who were staying there. My mother went every day together with our landlady to the field. They were working in the garden. And she could look, observe, and even recognise the faces of those people who were there looting the remaining few houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell me whether in the area --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And I will ask the usher to show the witness again the map P803 which is "Hrustovo-Vrhpolje overview."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether in the area which you can see on the map whether there were any -- any mosques.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes of course there were. In this area, there was a few mosques. In the Hrustovo village, there were two, one in the -- between Merdjanovici and Seferovici and the second one outside the village of Hrustovo in the direction of the Kljevci village. Then there was another one in the central part of the Muslim part of Tomina. And one was in Vrhpolje, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to these mosques?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A few days later they no longer existed. During the period while we were staying in the Tomina village, they were shelled.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: First would you be so kind and once again, take the highlighter and make crosses where the mosques were.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Madam Richterova. For the record, the Chamber indicates that the witness has put four crosses on the map, and he's being asked now to put next to each one of these crosses his initials. And Mr. Begic, please -- yesterday you indicated to us on the map the journey from your village to Vrhpolje Bridge. I would like you to put your initials as well on the route that you indicated to us yesterday, at the beginning, at the end of the route. Thank you. Just your initials, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. Yes, Madam Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said that a few days later they no longer existed. Can you explain to us what happened and what do you mean by "a few days later."

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I reached Tomina, the houses I used to live in are still there and some mosques could still be seen, particularly those in Hrustovo. Both of them were still intact. And then one day shortly after my arrival, it was in fact announced that the mosque would be shelled, and all of us watched the guiding of projectiles towards the mosque in the upper part of Hrustovo, here.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When he said that it was announced, who said that?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A patrol of soldiers passed through the village and said that we should refrain from being in the street because they would be shelling the mosque in Hrustovo from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And did you see what happened to this mosque?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After a few hits, they managed to hit the upper mosque in Hrustovo, which was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And did you see it by yourself?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What happened to the other mosques?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mosque in lower Hrustovo, I saw it standing one day and then the next day it was no longer standing. But I wasn't present -- I didn't witness it being destroyed by them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And the remaining two mosques?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mosque in Vrhpolje, again I didn't eyewitness its destruction. And in Tomina, the village I was staying in, I would pass by the mosque every day, because it wasn't far from the house. And one day neighbours, Muslims from the village came and told us that the night before at midnight their mosque had been destroyed. It was destroyed during the night while we were asleep.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You were in Tomina, and you stated that you stayed there for approximately during the end of June, beginning of July. Where did you go from Tomina?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One morning a civilian car passed through this village of Tomina with a loudspeaker system, and an officer that I knew was ordering all the inhabitants of Tomina, that is, all the refugees from other villages, should be brought in front of the Palma coffee bar and that we should gather there within 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: After you gathered in front of this cafe, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Buses came to fetch us, and all the inhabitants -- which means men, women, and children -- they were transferred that same day to the Krings camp in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How would you describe briefly this Krings camp?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Krings camp was a rather large hall with metal walls and roof. It was empty inside. There was just a concrete floor. In front of the camp was a reception desk that was probably used by the commander of the camp and by the guards. It was just an empty -- large empty hall. I did not know what the building had been used for before, so I'm unable to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were you provided with bedding?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you receive food?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you have water?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you have toilets?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that people were taken outside, those who wanted to use the toilet. But I personally didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Krings camp?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The morning we arrived -- so we stayed together inside with the women, children, the elderly, the sick, until the next morning, I think, when very early in the morning they ordered all the women, children, the old people, the pensioners, to get into the vehicles that had come for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know where they were taken?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time they didn't tell us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you learn later where were they taken?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only after I went to another camp. I heard from other detainees there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What did you hear?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That all of them had been transferred via Gracanica to a free part of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And how -- you men, how long did you stay in Krings?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, they made a list of all the people who remained in the camp for about two days, and then in the morning of the third day we were transported to another place. So we stayed for all of the next two days and one night.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Where were you transported?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came to fetch us with large Agrokomerc lorries with trailers, and there were some other men inside already. And then they drove us to in front of the sports hall in Sanski Most, where the detainees from the sports hall were loaded onto the trucks, and that day they transported us to Manjaca camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know what -- for what purposes, sir, Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was it prison?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were you interrogated in Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were you charged with anything during your stay in the camp?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was interrogated, as were all the other detainees, applying the habitual procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left on the 16th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Under which circumstances you left the Manjaca camp? You do not understand my question. Were you released --

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not quite.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were you released from the camp?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Richterova, you can -- you're authorised to put a direct question. And if you don't want to do it, I'll do it myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were you taken by the Red Cross from the camp?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you were transferred to where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They took us to the town of Karlovac in Croatia, where we were put up.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now I -- I've finished this part of questioning, and I will move to the year 1996, when exhumations took place in Sanski Most municipality?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness our exhibit, which already been exhibited under P791. If I may have a look at the copy. Do you have the B/C/S version of this, please. Your Honour, we managed to obtain better copies of this exhibit. So I would kindly ask if it is possible to replace the previous copy which is not legible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Madam Richterova. Yes. What I was going to ask you, actually, is what do you want to prove precisely by the series of questions you intend putting to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because it may well be that what you are going to ask the witness is not contested by the Defence. I don't know. These are the exhumations. I'm not exactly quite -- I don't quite know how -- how interested the Defence is in the details. Let's hear Madam Richterova first tell us what she wants to prove.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I will. I only want to ask the witness whether he can recognise any of these names and whether these people were on the bridge that particular day with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: If I may to ask you -- and maybe we can also put the document on the ELMO. If you can have a look at the last page and the page before. It's page 19 and 20. And it -- on the page 19, it reads: "On the basis of statements on recognition, the following persons were identified." Can you have a look on the list of 15 names and tell us whether you are able to recognise any name. And when I say "any name," I am referring to the date of 31st of May when you were -- when you marched from Begici to Vrhpolje Bridge.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, under number 3, Begic Irfan. He is the man that I said was shot with a pistol before we arrived at the bridge. Number 4, Muhamed Dizdarevic is one of the three sons and a father who were also on the bridge. Number 11, Ismet Dizdarevic, the father of the three mentioned boys. 12, Mirsad Dizdarevic, the second oldest among the three sons. Number 13, Miralem Ceric, the man who stayed behind me at the bridge on the Sanica River. Number 14, Hakija Begic, the man who was with me at the bridge. And number 15, Fuad Begic, who was standing right next to me on the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. I have the last question relating to the event on 31st of May. Did any of the people who were taken to the bridge, to your knowledge did they have weapons?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean on that day?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I mean that day or the day before -- or days before.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you or to your knowledge the other people, did they participate in any kind of military resistance? And I am also again referring to these 20 people who were taken towards the Vrhpolje bridge.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. I have very last question or set of questions. Apart from the investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor, were you questioned by other authorities?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And I am now referring to authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in Bosnia and Herzegovina I made statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you remember who took these statements?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Mr. Adil Draganovic and Mr. Zijad ...

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: May I show the witness his two statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please do, Madam Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You may use my copies or yours. And if you can show the very last pages of these statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you were interviewed, did you sign after the interview the statements?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Are these signatures your own?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The two persons who were present during your interviews and who interviewed you, did they sign these statements in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I do not have more questions, and I concluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Richterova. Who is going to proceed first? Yes. Mr. Begic, you are now going to be cross-examined by Madam Fauveau-Ivanovic, who is the co-counsel representing General Talic. I want you to understand that counsel is here to do her duty, to represent her client and to defend her client, and that therefore you are expected to answer all the questions that she puts to you except and unless I tell you not to. Madam Fauveau, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the registrar give the witness P757.2.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, yesterday you said that Kenjari and Begici were inhabited by Muslims; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that there was another hamlet in addition to these two hamlets that was a Serb hamlet.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us the name of that Serb hamlet.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between the village of Begici and Kenjari there were two hamlets inhabited by Serbs. One was called Stojnovici, and not far from that hamlet there was another hamlet called Cosici.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And these two hamlets are not marked on this map; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they're not there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said yesterday that your Serb neighbours set up checkpoints. Is it not true that Muslims also set up checkpoints in their villages and hamlets?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true they set up a checkpoint at the village of Crnojevici, in our hamlet there was no checkpoint. And as for the other more removed hamlets near the villages of Hrustovo and Vrhpolje, I didn't go there at the time so I was not able to see.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't know whether there were any checkpoints at Hrustovo and Vrhpolje.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the Serbs set up checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not able to say exactly when.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us approximately? Was it in February, March, April?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think it was before March. Possibly in April, mid-April, but I'm unable to tell you with precision.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that a certain Jadranko Palija was at one of these checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us where this checkpoint was where Jadranko Palija was manning -- the one that Jadranko Palija was manning.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'll mark it. It was the village of Crnojevici and here was Cosici. And the road leading from Begici to Kenjari passed through this Crnojevici. And the two were linked, Crnojevici and Cosici. And at this crossroads there was a checkpoint set up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just for the record, the Chamber indicates that the witness has marked on document P757.2 the place he was asked to indicate in the question put to him by Madam Fauveau. He's being asked by the Trial Chamber to put his initials next to where he put the markings. Now, Mr. Cayley, since he's now put his initials and put markings, you will need to replace this one. And it becomes --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We were just discussing that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. I mean, if you have another map which you can bring forward that will replace the 757.2, and this will become DT15, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Yes, Madam Fauveau, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did Jadranko Palija come from one of these two hamlets, Cosici or Stojinovici?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where he came from -- where he was from?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I pointed out a moment ago, we were on good terms with Vido Krlic's family, to whom I surrendered when I left the water. And we worked together in the fields. We shared the same machinery. And Mrs. Andja Krlic had a daughter called Suzana, and Jadranko Palija was Suzana's boyfriend, so that in our daily conversations we could hear the name -- his name used by Mrs. Krlic. But I never heard actually where he was born.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where Jadranko Palija was from September 1991 to April 1992?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this story, I heard once that he lived in Croatia. And after the war broke out in Croatia, he withdrew to Bosnia, and he was stationed during that period in our area, in our area.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And when did he arrive in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm unable to say exactly when.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us approximately.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know when he arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that there were certain soldiers at these checkpoints, and you said that they belonged to the 6th Brigade. How did you know that they belonged to the 6th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have already said, over the media one could hear that the 6th Brigade was deployed in the area. No mention was made of any other units; at least, I don't know of any others. They wore the insignia on their clothing of the Serb army. And I believe there was an indication that it was the 6th Krajina Brigade, but I'm not sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that there were symbols of the Serb army on their uniforms, do you mean that already in April there were symbols of the Serb army?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And what were those symbols?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there was the flag, the three colours -- the three-coloured flag of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: The flag of Serbia? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you describe that flag for me, please.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were three colours with an eagle in the middle, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the month of April 1992, the JNA, the Yugoslav army, still existed, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you allow for the possibility that these men that you saw that were wearing Serb symbols on their uniform belonged to certain paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not be able to say, because I don't remember very well those symbols, so I'd rather not assert anything regarding the symbols and which unit they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: But would you allow for the possibility that this was not the regular Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. The witness has answered the question. It's been put to him a number of times at this point. I know where Ms. Fauveau is trying to go with this cross-examination. He's already answered very clearly "I would not be able to say because I don't remember very well these symbols, so I'd rather not assert anything." So he's already indicated that that's as far as he can go. He can't allow for any other possibilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau. The objection is sustained if you have nothing to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that army units arrived for the first time in your village on the 25th of May, 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And how many soldiers arrived on the 25th of May?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us roughly how many.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot, because in those days the flora and fauna well developed. So because of this great quantity of greenery, I was not able to judge the exact number of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You personally, did you see those soldiers?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And were those soldiers wearing the same symbols as those you described a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not be able to say because at that point in time, when they were entering the village for the first time, I managed to get away and hide next to the river, as my house was very close to the river.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you cannot identify the people who arrived in your village on the 25th of May; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can identify them on the basis of conversations with my mother, because my mother also knew some of them who entered the village, who mistreated her and beat her, who killed my dog.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us the name of those people that your mother identified.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Dusko Savic, from Kljevci.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Anyone else?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was enough, because he was in the house with her, and she wasn't interested in the others.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And this Dusko Savic was living in Kljevci, was he?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He went to school with me for eight years.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And in the period preceding the war in Bosnia, at the very beginning of 1992 he was still in Kljevci, was he?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that the soldiers came one more time before the 31st of May to your village. Could you tell us when this was, the second time that they arrived.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after two days, they came to the village again -- actually, to the upper part of the Begici hamlet -- where Ismet Kurbegovic, Hakija Begic, Sacir Begic were beaten. And according to what they said, they had charges against them allegedly that they had, and I quote, that Ismet Begic owned a sniper rifle, that Sacir Begic had fed some Green Berets in his basement, Hakija Begic was charged of having a hand-held rocket launcher in his attic, a zolja.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: These people, Ismet Kurbegovic, Ismet Begic, and Sacir Begic, were they beaten the first day when the soldiers came or the second time they came?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were beaten the first time and the second time. And they were beaten by Ranko Cosic, Vico Ilic, Bosko Stojnovic. People from the hamlets of Stovnovici and Cosici.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So these three persons whose names you mentioned, were your neighbours; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And in the period prior to the war, between January and April 1992 were these people living in Stojinovici and Cosici?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see these persons beating Kurbegovic and Sacir and Ismet Begic?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw those three gentlemen the moment when we got together on the 31st, and I saw what they looked like.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you saw them on the 31st of May, 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And these three persons were wearing a uniform.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Those three persons, did they have the symbols on their uniform that you described, that is, the Serb flag with an eagle?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm unable to tell you in detail, but they were wearing military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: All the soldiers that arrived in your village that day, were they wearing the same uniforms?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The day they rounded us up, on the 31st, there were different ones. There were those in SMB, the normal colour of uniforms, and camouflage uniforms, military camouflage uniforms. Some were wearing a helmet that day, and others had different hats on their heads. So I didn't look closely at their insignia.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So in fact the people were wearing different uniforms and wearing different symbols.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about the uniforms. I didn't say anything about the symbols. It is well known to everyone that there are camouflage military uniforms and regular military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that at the time almost all men were wearing some sort of uniform?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke of a lieutenant who was a commander of a unit and who ordered Jadranko Palija to take you to the Vrhpolje Bridge.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: How did you know that he was a lieutenant?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wore the lieutenant's insignia on his shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you describe this lieutenant's insignia.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On your shoulder, one wore an epaulette with a gold braid on the edges. And in between, there were two arrows with a star, maybe two stars. I did my military service a long time ago, so I've forgotten. But at the time I knew he was a lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it not true that in Yugoslavia before 1990 all men were members of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So also you didn't know that all men had a uniform at home.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived at the Vrhpolje bridge, could you tell us how many people you found there when you arrived.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we arrived at the bridge, one could notice a bunker at the crossroads towards the villages of Ilija and Tomina. And in the bunker around it, there were quite a few soldiers. We were taken over by five or six of them, who were standing right next to the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: These soldiers that you're talking about, were they regular soldiers?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that roughly in the period end of May, beginning of June there was fighting between Muslims and Serbs around the village of Vrhpolje?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: What is the distance between your village of Begici and Vrhpolje?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three or four kilometres. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: After this tragic event on the Vrhpolje bridge when you arrived at your Serb neighbour's house and when this officer came to take you to Tomina, could you tell me whether during your transfer to Tomina you were mistreated.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And when you say that there was an officer, do you mean that that was an officer of the army?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Of the regular army?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say. He had rank insignia. I hadn't known him before.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you were interrogated at the Tomina school, the elementary school at Tomina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your written statement of the 16th of April, you said: [In English] "I was taken to the SDS headquarters near the school." [Interpretation] I should like to know whether you were taken to the school or to a house next to the school.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they took me to the school. But I don't remember saying that it was the SDS headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: In any event, that is what Judge Draganovic wrote. You said that certain mosques were destroyed while you were staying at Tomina.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You personally saw the destruction of the mosque in Hrustovo, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether in Hrustovo too there was fighting between Muslims and Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of a battle in Hrustovo. According to stories of some Serb soldiers who came to Tomina and on the basis of inhabitants that heard this from Serb soldiers, it was said that in Hrustovo there was a paramilitary unit consisting of several young men who tried to put up resistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you allow for the possibility that there was an armed conflict between Muslims and Serbs in Hrustovo.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It couldn't be said --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Before the witness answers, when? When?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While he was staying at Tomina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Give a date. If you're referring to an armed conflict in Hrustovo, give an approximate date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I took it that the previous question referred to the destruction of the mosque at a time when he saw it himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, quite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you are referring to that particular point in time. No?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was in Tomina for about Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. a month. I'm referring to this period of one month. I'm not talking of a conflict that lasted one or two days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So now you know more or less what you are being asked, Mr. Begic. Please as far as regards a time frame.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'm not aware of that, of any fighting.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally see the destruction of other mosques, apart from the one in Hrustovo?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have already said, I watched one being destroyed personally. And the one in the village of Merdjanovici, I saw it intact one day and then the next day it was no longer standing. But I didn't watch the shelling of that mosque.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My question related to the actual act of destruction of the mosque. As for the mosque in Tomina, you didn't see it being destroyed either, did you?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the ruins afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: But the destruction itself you did not see.

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Just as I said, they destroyed it during the night, so that no one could see exactly who destroyed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: As regards the mosque in Hrustovo, the destruction of which you observed, you said that certain soldiers came and announced that they were going to destroy the mosque; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They passed through the village of Tomina and said that we should get away from the streets because they would from the direction of the Vrhpolje Bridge target the mosque in Hrustovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Those soldiers that you saw passing through Tomina, were they also wearing these uniforms with the Serb flag and eagle symbol on their sleeves?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in a car. They were sitting in a car and driving through the village they said this, so that it was impossible to see those symbols.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: May just raise a very brief point of order, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think I recall a time a few weeks ago when Madam Fauveau was responsible for a witness and Mr. De Roux started making objections and I believe it was Mr. Cayley who said only one counsel should be responsible for a witness and make objections during that witness's testimony. And I thought we established a rule in that regard. This being Ms. Richterova's witness, I think she --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you are right, Mr. Ackerman. You are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, as you know, Ms. Korner and I are lead Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It doesn't change anything. The witness was in the hands of Madam Richterova, and I would have expected her to stand up. I mean, take it as a rule. I did correct Mr. De Roux when he did that. And not correcting you -- I'm just drawing your attention. It did escape me at the time. But please make sure that once the witness is in the hands of one counsel, it remains in the hands of that counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not a -- I know you did not do that out of disrespect, just as Mr. De Roux did not do that out of disrespect to the Tribunal. Mr. Ackerman, we need to break now for half an hour. You're going to cross-examine the witness immediately after. How long -- can I ask you how long do you expect to conduct your cross-examination for more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Trbojevic is handling this witness, and I'll let him answer your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will not cross-examine this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So basically, Mr. Cayley, be prepared to introduce the next witness immediately after the break. We will resume at 11.00 sharp. Thank you. Oh, I'm sorry. Is there a re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could I let you know that at the next session. It will be very little, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Is there going to be a re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I have very brief questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: But just for the record, that Julian Nicholls joined the Prosecution team in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. And welcome. I understand you will be taking over the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Mr. Begic, there are a few final questions that the Prosecution would like to ask you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, Madam Fauveau asked you whether -- I better say that you answered Madam Fauveau that the soldiers on the bridge on the Vrhpolje Bridge on the 31st of May were not regular. To her question "were they regular," you answered "no." Who were they?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the question was put to the witness in direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think she is -- I think Madam Fauveau is right. If you want, we'll check the transcript. We can go back and check the transcript. But I do myself recall that you did put a direct question to that effect, you know, what -- whether they were -- they wore uniforms and whether they -- according to the witness, what uniforms they were, whether he could identify them as --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I agree I asked this question. But Madam Fauveau asked whether they were regular soldiers, and the witness answered no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. He's answered no.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is that the cross-examination is a function of the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But what do you want to ask the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I only want him to answer if they were not regular what did they -- what did he mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you have already put that question to him on examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: If you are satisfied with his answer, I don't need to ask any more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau, I think the questions that were asked, both during the examination-in-chief and during the cross-examination, have procured the answers that the witness had for us or was prepared to give us, and I don't think we can allow any further questions in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wanted really only to clarify that point. Otherwise, if it is clear, I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me put the question myself. Mr. Begic, you have been questioned on those soldiers and what they were wearing and who they belonged to by the Prosecution, as well by the Defence. Do you have any further information that you could give to this Trial Chamber to make it easier for us or make it possible for us to identify any military corps or whatever that these soldiers could have belonged to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I would add something. When answering the Prosecutor whether I recognised them as regulars or not, I knew these young men. They lived in their homes, and their age didn't correspond to the age of regular soldiers. And in my statement, I omitted the name of Nenad Kaurin, who wore -- he was dressed in blue. I think he was the reserve police force and he wore a blue beret on his head, so that I believe it wasn't all -- that this was the regular army corps -- that it was not the regular army corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you answer any questions, please look at me and I will tell you whether to answer or not. Yes, Madam Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you said "he was in a blue uniform," was the other soldiers also in blue uniform?

utterances.speaker: RAJIF BEGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that he wore it. Others wore military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And when you say "military uniform," what colour was the military uniform?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He has already answered that question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You put already the question to him during your examination-in-chief, even the colours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. And I apologise. It's only that now he mentioned this blue colour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But it seems to be the only -- the only person who was wearing that blue uniform or -- which he relates to the police rather than to the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No. Your Honour, I do not have any further question in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Begic, I -- that brings us to the end of your testimony here. On behalf of my colleagues, the other two Judges, myself, and the Tribunal, I would like to thank you for having coming here to give evidence. You will now be escorted out of the courtroom by the usher and given all the attention you require to return back to where you have requested to return.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley and Mr. Ackerman and Madam Fauveau, the next witness we will have to take some time to prepare the courtroom. He is a pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Image distortion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Well, no voice distortion. One matter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No voice distortion. No. You didn't mention it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: One point of order, Your Honour. Mr. Nicholls, who's leading this witness, is not going to be available next week. He has to go on a mission to Bosnia. So I will do the re-examination, if that is satisfactory to you, if there is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. No. No. Definitely. I mean, it's -- it goes without saying that ... Okay. How long do you expect your examination-in-chief to last, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm fairly certain I'll finish today quickly. I guess two hours or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: His statement is quite a short one, you know, so I would imagine that we could finish today. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I spoke to representatives of the OTP, and I asked whether they agreed that I do my cross-examination on Monday if they finish their examination-in-chief earlier today so that I can start on Monday, in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I take it you're cooperating.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does that mean that the moment the examination-in-chief is finished, that's all for today, or that -- in other words, you are going to go first.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. That's okay with Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And while waiting for the witness, I should like to inform the Chamber that I spoke to the representatives of the Registry, who informed me that the decision regarding Mr. Zecevic will be made today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Fauveau. I will be checking on that myself later on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, because I've finished my witness, will you excuse me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Madam Richterova. And thank you. Have a nice weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, Mr. Cayley, once we're finished with BT23, the next one will be 7.10; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let me check, Your Honours, so that I give you accurate information. It's 7.100. I think you probably are meaning the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, 7.100. Okay. All right. Yes, usher, I think we are ready. You can bring the witness, escort him into the courtroom, and we can start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Look at me, please, sir. Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You've been summoned to give evidence before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And before you do so, it's the rule of this Tribunal that you make a solemn declaration to tell us the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The declaration is contained on a piece of paper that the usher is going to hand to you. Please take it in your hands and read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Before you start giving evidence, may I give you some information. First of all, the Trial Chamber - that's myself and the other two Judges - were informed by the Prosecution that you asked for certain protective measures, such as that no one would be able to see you giving evidence. Your image will be distorted. Your name will not be used. You are given a number, a pseudonym, and you will be referred to by that number in the records of these proceedings and also in -- in the records of these proceedings. The procedure before this Tribunal is as follows: The Prosecution will first ask you a series of questions. When the Prosecution has finished what we refer to as the direct question -- the direct examination or examination-in-chief, then it will be the turn of the Defence teams to cross-examine you. Now, the Prosecution team is to your right, and the gentleman nearest to you, Mr. Nicholls, will be the counsel, the lawyer, who will be examining you for the Prosecution. The two Defence teams are at your left. And in the front row is the Defence team for Radoslav Brdjanin. I can't tell you as from now who will be conducting the cross-examination but -- it will be Mr. Trbojevic. And later on you will be cross-examined also by Madam Fauveau, representing General Talic. So having said that, I invite Mr. Nicholls to start with his examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know at which stage we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. You do that straight away. Sir, you're going to be handed a paper, on which there is your name written. I want you to look at it and then tell me without mentioning your name whether that is your name or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is. Usher, please show it to the Defence teams and then to us, and it will be introduced in the records under seal as ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As P805.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, now, please remember whichever questions I ask you not to mention your name or the names of your family members. I'm going to quickly ask you a few questions about your background and then we will move on to events in Sanski Most in 1992. You were born --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, if I could request private session at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes. We can go in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the translation was, [redacted], to [redacted], my friends took me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I can clarify that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But we can go back to private session, but I need an explanation. Because to me it doesn't make sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We can clarify this event. But I agree it needs to be clarified. But in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So when it is time to go back to that event, Mr. Nicholls please tell me and we'll go into private session again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think we should go into private session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We go into private session now, straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Could you now describe the way relations changed after the war began in Croatia. And remember, as we spoke about yesterday, if you could try to just answer the question that I ask you, and then we'll move on and I'll continue to ask you questions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: The situation changed. The Muslims didn't want to join and go -- join the army to -- in the war in Croatia and fight in Croatia and the Serbs didn't want to have contacts with us any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what exactly did the relations become like? There was no contact, or was there any animosity or hostility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: These Serbs went to war to the front in Croatia. When they would return, they would be shooting. And the entire Croat and Muslim population was afraid of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to move on a little bit now and talk about May 1992. At any point was there an order made for people to turn over any weapons they possessed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: On the 25th of May, 1992, in the morning two couriers came and asked the Muslims to hand over their weapons in the central building in Lukavica. And that this -- these weapons be taken to Fajtovci to the Crisis Staff in Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Can you tell me who those two couriers were, where they were from.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: They took the weapons from Lukavica to Fajtovci. Kalender Ismet and Alibegovic and Halilovic Hamed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry. Let me ask that again. Who made the order? Who did those couriers represent when they came and told people to turn over weapons -- told the Muslims to turn over weapons? Was it military police, civilian? Who made that order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: It was Dragan Prastalo and the Serbian Crisis Staff from Fajtovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were there any threats made -- stated of what would happen if these weapons were not turned over?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: That by 10.00 if we don't hand over the weapons, the village would be shelled. And the Muslims collected the weapons and went towards Fajtovci. And two or three kilometres between Fajtovci and Lukavica, they were stopped and captured.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could -- the interpreter apologises. Could the witness repeat his last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. We have a problem with the interpretation. You said, "That by 10.00, if we don't hand over the weapons, the village would be shelled." Then you continued saying: "The Muslims collected the weapons and went towards Fajtovci. And two or three kilometres between Fajtovci --" the rest the interpreters couldn't hear. So could you continue from there, please. You did mention that someone was stopped or whatever.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When they came from Fajtovci to hand over the weapons, and the weapons were collected, and three people took the weapons from Lukavica to Fajtovci. And halfway between Fajtovci and Lukavica, they were stopped by the Serbian guard, the Serb patrol. And they were also captured. They were to lie on the ground, and the Serbs took the weapons that they brought. And two or three hours -- after two or three hours of interrogation, they were let free, after they -- the weapons were handed in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I move on, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were there any checks made to make sure that all the weapons were collected? In other words, were houses or other property searched in your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: A couple of days later, several soldiers came. They surrounded the village, between 50 and 100 of them, and they ordered that the whole village be evacuated, all the men should leave. And then with all the male inhabitants, they went from one house to the next searching each and every household.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Was your house searched?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: Of course, yes. They searched my house as well and all the other houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And after that point, were there any weapons kept by Muslims in your village to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: I think that they didn't dare, because the order was if anybody kept a weapon or something like that and if it was found, that that person would be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to ask you again, talking about this same time period, whether there were any checkpoints set up around your village and in that general area you pointed out to us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: For a Muslim to leave the village, he had to address Dragan Prastalo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So there were checkpoints set up around the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we lost a whole bunch of testimony. There was no translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The translation came later, as I get it. But if you doubt whether we had the whole lot, I will ask the witness to repeat what he said. I can't tell him --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A part of the sentence was certainly lost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Could you help us more, Madam Fauveau, if you can, because he said "For a Muslim to leave the village, he had to address Dragan Prastalo." And the question was: "Now I'd like to ask you again, talking about this same time period whether there were any checkpoints set around your village and in that general area you pointed out to us." What was your answer? Let's leave it at --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't like to make any suggestions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes, sir. Could you answer that question again, please. The question was: "Now, I would like to ask you again. Talking about this same time period whether there were any checkpoints set up around your village and in that general area you pointed out to us." What was your answer? Could you repeat it, please. Again it's a problem of -- it's a problem of interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologies. I didn't switch on my microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At junctures, checkpoints were put up. There were four. One was at Dragan Prastalo's place [redacted] [redacted]. The whole village or -- rather if anyone from the village wanted to go out, he had to ask Dragan Prastalo who would give a certificate or a Serb soldier to escort him, to do whatever he wanted to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
