utterances.text: Thank you. Who manned those checkpoints? Who was in charge of those checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: They were local Serbs. And very often Martic's men would come wearing olive-grey uniforms, camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were these people you refer to as local Serbs in uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: They were all in uniforms. Even Lazo, a boy of 14, he was wearing a uniform. Dragan's son, who was ten years old had a uniform. Children were wearing uniforms and carrying weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And again, the only way to pass through one of these checkpoints as a Muslim was to get prior permission and get a certificate; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd now like you to talk a little bit about any shelling of villages which you observed in May 1992 in this region of your village. Did you see any villages being shelled during that period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: That day when we were handing over our weapons, the Serbs shelled Okrec and Brijest, and we saw the shells falling and the dust flying around. When a couple of shells hit Brijest, we heard crying. My neighbour and relative of mine, [redacted], and I went to Brijest, and over there we found a cow of Ivezic Ivan that had been wounded, and the glass was broken on two houses and the facade damaged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Nicholls. At one point in time he mentioned -- "and very often Martic's men would come wearing olive-grey uniforms, camouflage uniforms." Who was Martic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. There were quite -- people from our area going for exercises with Martic. And when they arrived in the village, they were the ones that were feared the most. They were well trained karatists, as far as I was able to judge by their appearance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Back to the shelling very quickly. What did you and your family do in response to this shelling? How did it change the way -- your way of life there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: Every night at dusk, we went to the woods below our houses. We slept there. And then in the morning, we returned. Even babies and old women up to 80, we had to take them with us, because there was shooting all night by the guards at the checkpoints and the other Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to ask you some questions about arrests during this period. Were any Muslim men from your village arrested in May, early June 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: There were a couple of men arrested before me. I too was arrested in June. In the morning at 7.00, they came to fetch me; some 15 soldiers wearing camouflage uniforms. When I heard the bus, I fled to some bushes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go into private session, Madam Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You were describing the room that you were placed in in Lusci Palanka. Can you continue to describe that room.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: From that upper floor, they took us to a police station one by one, and then after interrogation they brought us back to the basement of the house that we had been brought to the first time. When they took me, I was interrogated for a while and then a soldier hit me and I fell, and then they hit me a couple more times with their hands and feet - I don't know what with --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You said you were interrogated. Excuse me. What types of questions were you asked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: Whether we were feeding the Green Berets, did we have any weapons, whether we were members of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And again, just to be clear, who was doing this questioning to you and who was beating you at this time? Without mentioning names.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: I was interrogated by the police commander, [redacted]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: [redacted]. And I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have to redact this. Yes. Go ahead. We will redact it in due course, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You said some other men were brought to that building with you. Were they also beaten, or were they not beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: And they were even beaten more. I was lucky because they knew me. They had more blood on them than I did. They mostly beat me in the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How long did this last, what you're describing, this beating and questioning and interrogation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: I don't know. When he hit me here, I fell on the floor. And then they kicked me a couple of times and with their hands. I don't know exactly how long this went on for.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then what happened next? After this beating ended, where were you taken or what did you do next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: Then they took me to the basement of the house that we had been brought to the first time, originally. After that, they took me and [redacted] to Sanski Most to the Betonirka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: They released [redacted]and allowed him to go home.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We don't need to mention names at this point. Tell me what happened when you were taken to Betonirka.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: As I was entering Betonirka, two soldiers hit me on the shoulders with their rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And just to be clear, you're talking about the Betonirka garage.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, the garages of the Betonirka. I entered there. There were up to 30 other men there who were all deformed, they had been beaten up on their heads and faces before I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you could continue. You were beginning to tell us how you were beaten immediately upon arrival there. Can you continue telling us what happened to you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: As I was entering the garage, they hit me a couple of times. They kicked me in the behind and shoved me into the garage. When I fell, I saw up to 30 men in the garage that were detained there, and they all had traces of beating on their faces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you describe the garage that was holding you and these approximately 30 men in total. How -- how large was it? What type of garage was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: The garage was about 3 and a half or 4 metres long by 2 and a half metres. There were 30 men inside. When the door is closed, you couldn't breathe inside, because there was no air coming in from anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Was there a window in that garage you were kept in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: It had a window that was covered with metal, and you couldn't see through it. It was a small window. It was a small one, about 20 by 50 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But you couldn't open it to let any light in. Could you open it to let any air in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: No one dared even think of it, never mind open it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were there any toilets or showers or other facilities in that garage you were kept in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: During the day, while we were in prison, if the door of the garage was open we could go to the field toilet. And when the garage was closed, there was a bucket in the corner where we had to relieve ourselves. Because if someone would knock on the door to ask for the garage to be opened, he would immediately be beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How often was that garage door open to allow people to go in and out and to let some air in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: It depended on the guard. If the guard was in a good mood, he would open it for half an hour when he was on duty. And when lunch came -- we had it around 11.00 or 12.00. I don't know exactly because they took away my watch and all documents, so we didn't know the time at all whether it was daytime or night-time or what time it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You talked about lunch just now. Can you describe the food that you would be given when you were held in that garage.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: The lunch consisted of a very thin soup, like water. And a piece of bread.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were you given anything else during the day or during a 24-hour period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: Yes, beatings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were you given any other food?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: No, none.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what about water? What was provided to you to drink while you were held there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: We would get some water in dirty glass bottles, but we had to drink it because it was so hot and there was no air inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Talking about the other people who were imprisoned in the garage with you, what types of people were they? Were these young people, old people, soldiers, civilians? If you could describe the people you were confined with.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: All the people -- there were some younger ones, some older ones. There was a 35-year-old man with a son who was not more than 15 years old. And when they beat his father, he would always cry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you said earlier, I think, that everybody was beaten; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: They beat everyone. They beat up two men so badly that we had to make room for them to lie down, as they seemed to have all their bones broken. They would cry and moan all night long.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Was there room for anybody else to lie down while these two men were lying down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: No. We were mostly sitting down, even during the night. That is how we slept, because there wasn't enough room for us. And there were two other garages. And I saw those garages and the people coming out when we were having lunch. They, too, were full of people, just as we were in our garage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And you talked about how you were beaten when you arrived. Were you also interrogated? And can you describe that interrogation without mentioning names.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: They took me for interrogation. I recognised some friends there who used to work there. I used to have contact with them. Maybe that helped me. And they let me go. I spent two nights there. And on the third day, they released me from prison. First they beat me, and afterwards this friend, I suppose he told them not to beat me any more because he knew me very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: While they were beating you, what types of questions were being asked of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: They said -- they cursed Alija. "Where are your Green Berets? Why didn't you join the army to fight the Croats?"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I don't think anybody in the circumstances you've described can be -- could be described as lucky. But is what you're saying that you felt that you were more fortunate than many of the other people who were placed in that garage with you, because you knew some of the people who were beating you? Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: I knew three or four of them. One of them was even my neighbour and a good friend of mine from before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you think -- I'm just trying to clarify -- that because some of these people had been your friends, that's why you were released after two days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: I think that is what it was, but I haven't found out anything to this day, anything specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. What happened to some of the other people in the garages while you were there? Were any people taken away? Did people arrive while you were there? Was this a transitory place, in that sense?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: There were quite a number of people that were taken away and that never returned; others that went for interrogation, they came back broken up. Two or three were carried in and thrown into the garage, and we would take them over and assist them as much as we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And were the people who were running this camp and interrogating you, beating you, were they wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: They all had uniforms. Summer uniforms, shirts and olive-grey or camouflage trousers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: After what you've just described, this period you spent in Betonirka garage, what happened next? You stated you were released after two days. What did you do next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: Together with another Hasim, I was released. And he was from Kamengrad. And a friend of his, as he worked at the petrol station, drove us to Donji Kamengrad. And then I continued on foot for 8 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: As I was given a certificate allowing me to pass so that the Serb army would let me pass through checkpoints and other crossings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to ask you very briefly about what you know of the Lukavica mosque. I believe you saw that mosque on the 2nd of August, 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: That is correct. The mosque was blown up before I saw it. Who Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. did it, I don't know, nor did I see it. On the 2nd of August, when I drove these people who had been killed, I saw that the mosque's roof had been damaged, the glass broken. Everything was in ruins.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you know when that damage was done to the mosque, when it had been blown up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: It must have been during the night in July, as far as I can recollect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm now going to ask you some questions about the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can we go into private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I was going to suggest it myself, actually. Please let's go into private session now. Yes. I suppose we're coming to the events of the 1st of August?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. It needs to be in private session for sure.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: We had to fill out a questionnaire that we would be leaving everything we have to the Republic of Srpska to pay our telephone bills, to pay our taxes, land tax, electricity bills, and then we would be allowed to leave in a convoy which would go to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Where did you have to fill out these forms or submit these documents you've just told us about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: We had to do it in the municipality and Sanski Most. As these women who were so hurt, so miserable, I had to fill out all these forms and sign them -- also sign them for myself and for them too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And after you'd filled out those forms, you were granted permission to leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: Yes, we were allowed to leave. But not everybody left. Some women didn't leave. They had their relatives there, and they organised themselves, while we came -- we left for Dosci in a truck and a trailer, and from Dosci then we each one went our separate ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what of your property were you allowed to bring with you -- were you able to bring with you when you left? Were you able to bring anything from your home which you had to leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: We could take with us what we could put in our bags, but not more than that because there wasn't any place on the truck when there were 40 people on the truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And finally, when you were getting permission to move -- or to conduct the burial, were you ever given any reason for why this killing had taken place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: They didn't know themselves, but a woman said that -- one of my neighbours, that he had a rifle and machine-gun, but it was never found. But the Serbs, they would on guard throughout the night, and then the next night they shelled [redacted] house with two or three shells. The building was practically half demolished.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. One second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need -- Madam Registrar again we need to redact this particular part where he mentions the person's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: After you left your village on -- you said you had been given permission to leave and you would go on -- you were placed on a truck -- where did you -- you said you went to Dosci. Where did you go? How did you -- you don't need to tell me the country where you eventually ended up, but how were you able to leave?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I give you permission to be more direct, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: After that, you went on a convoy. You eventually made it to Travnik. And from there you left to the country where you now reside. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So yes -- but as I understand it, the Prosecution has finished with the examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And as I take it also, there is a tacit agreement between the Prosecution and Madam Fauveau that she would start her cross-examination on Monday. That entails, basically, that the witness will have to stay here the entire weekend. I don't know having heard the examination-in-chief if Madam Fauveau wants to cross-examine the witness and if it's still necessary to postpone the cross-examination till Monday. If you are in a position to tell me now, then tell me now. If you want to postpone your decision till after a break, we can have a break and you can tell me after.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to think it over during the break. And if I can, I will do it today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And that would be appreciated, Madam Fauveau, because it would spare this person having to remain here a whole two -- a whole weekend for possibly a very short cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my cross-examination will not be very long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I can imagine. This is why, I mean, I -- my experience tells me that. And I don't know if the Brdjanin Defence team is going to cross-examine the witness. My hunch is that you will not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we'll let you know after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we'll have a short break --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was going to ask a break that could be ten minutes longer, if we could have a 40-minute break, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Madam Fauveau. Certainly, Madam Fauveau. We'll have a 40-minute break, during which time you will have the chance to consult with your client, obviously. The same applies to you, Mr. Ackerman, and the rest of the team. I can anticipate more or less what the answer is going to be. So the session is adjourned -- the sitting is adjourned and we will resume at ten minutes past 1.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Trbojevic. I need to get familiarised. There is just one syllable extra that I can't handle. Yes, Mr. Trbojevic. Is that correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We've agreed that I will ask just three questions to the witness, and it will take only five minutes, and I'd like to complete that today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Trbojevic, for your cooperation and understanding. And Madam Fauveau, seeing you here, it means that you -- but I am not in any way trying to force your -- but I am sure you understand that if this witness can go back to his family today, it will be better than staying here.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I fully understand, and I hope that I will finish and leave -- be able to leave five minutes for Mr. Trbojevic at the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. Please proceed. You are going to be cross-examined now by Madam Fauveau, who is the counsel -- who is counsel for General Talic. Go ahead, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you said that before the war, relations between the Serbs and the Muslims were good; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you also said that relations became less good with the beginning of the war in Croatia and with the refusal of the Muslims to go and fight in Croatia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can it be said that the refusal of the Muslims to go and fight in Croatia preceded the degradation of relations between Muslims and Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: I know that there was a Serb who went to Croatia from our village. This went on for a couple of months. And he was killed in Croatia, and there was a funeral. All of us went to the funeral. His father said to us then, "I'd prefer if you Muslims had not come to attend this funeral, --" because from then on the situation became even worse.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the time of this funeral, had the Muslims already refused to go and fight in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Why should we go to kill?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke of three men who were carrying weapons from your village to Fajtovci, and you said that they were captured; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: But you personally were not present when they were arrested.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't see who arrested them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: Those people lived with me after the war as refugees. They are all still alive, and they can testify about that. In fact, one of those men has a Serb woman for his wife.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Gentleman, I'm not doubting what you said. I'm just asking whether you personally saw who arrested them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: I personally did not see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke of soldiers who came to search the houses in your village, and you said that the men had to leave the village. Did the women and children stay behind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: The women and children remained, and we went with those soldiers to search the houses. We stayed with the soldiers -- with some soldiers outside, while some of them went inside to search.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you were present during those searches.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know the soldiers who were carrying out the searches?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: There were some soldiers from outside. My neighbours said they were Martic men. And then there were some local Serbs dressed in military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you spoke about Martic's men, are you referring to paramilitaries coming from Knin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: Madam, I don't know. They were wearing camouflage uniforms. They were very capable men, and they kept frightening us with these Martic's men. So I can't really tell you. They never showed me the documents for me to see or for us to see their identity.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: But you are indeed talking to Martic, who was before the war a policeman in Knin. If you don't know, tell me you don't know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: No, madam. Those were people who went to train with Martic. One had a surname Martic and he was from Kruhari. He also wasn't went there for training. He was in Betonirka, and he beat us most, that particular man.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that those men went for training to Martic, this Martic, is he the Martic from Knin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: No. These were soldiers. I suppose Martic trained them, and they were all known as Martic's men. My Serb neighbours that I contacted with during the war, I couldn't go where I wanted for two or three months and they would bring me a sack of flour or something, and they said that they were Martic's men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau, I asked the witness the same question myself, and he told me straight and plain that he didn't know who this Martic was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall move on to another subject, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that almost all the men, even children, were wearing uniforms; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: Yes, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct to say that these uniforms differed, that they were not all wearing the same kind of uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: There were SMB and camouflage, summer uniforms, shirts with trousers, and these locals mostly wore SMB uniforms, whereas those coming from other places that I didn't know were in camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke of the shelling of Brijest. Do you know where those shells came from? Could you tell us where they came from.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: Those shells came from the direction of Fajtovci, where the Crisis Staff was. The village was called Vukse. Actually, it's a small village of a couple of houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: What was the population composition in Fajtovci?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: There was a school there. There were teachers. One of them was a Montenegrin, Mihail Sutovic. He was president of the Crisis Staff. But I think there were more Muslims, 60 or 70 per cent were Muslims, maybe even more. There were only two smaller villages that were Serbian. But in Fajtovci, there were mostly Muslim households.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And Brijest, is it a Muslim hamlet or a mixed hamlet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: Brijest had three Croat households and two Albanian families. And eight or 15 days after the shelling, men came from Podvrace and killed those two Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the people in Brijest were armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: I know. These were older people, Croats. All the young people had moved out a long time ago. Only a couple of households who didn't have the funds stayed behind, and they're still living there, and the two or three of them that are left can come and testify as to what happened there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke of your arrest in June. Do you know who the people were that arrested you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: They were people from Palanka. The military police. They were wearing blue uniforms and in camouflage SMB uniforms. In fact, I knew two or three of them that went to school with me. They were from Palanka, Bosniaks. They are neighbouring villages above Palanka.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Those people that were wearing blue uniforms, did they belong to the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: There were some that used to be in the civilian police -- in the regular police, but some came from Slovenia, Dekici I know their names, that they were also there. And they wore the same uniforms. Now, whether they were admitted as regulars, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you were then taken to Lusci Palanka, first to a house and then to a police station; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And at the police station, you were interrogated, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true to say that you were interrogated by policemen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: They all wore police uniforms and those camouflage ones. I think they were policemen.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: How much time did you spend in Betonirka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: In the garage in Betonirka?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: Two nights and a day. I was released about 4.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who were the guards at Betonirka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: I don't know the guards. I know the people that interrogated me.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And the people who interrogated you, were they policemen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: Two of them were policemen. There were some reserve policemen too. There was the chief of the Crisis Staff -- I knew him too, and so on. By sight. These were people who held key positions in the past. They worked in the municipalities. They were police commanders, police officers in peacetime, before the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you left Betonirka, you returned to your village, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you had a certificate to be able to pass through the checkpoints; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: I just had permission to return to my home, and I had to hand in that permission down there to local Serbs, to Dragan Prastalo.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And along the road from Sanski Most to your village, did you have any problems on your way back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: A Serb went with us. He drove us as far as Donji Kamengrad, and he knew this man who was in prison in Donji Kamengrad. He -- we got off there, and then I went on to my house on foot. And there were no problems. It was dusk, and as soon as I heard a car approach I would hide in the bushes, and that is how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke of a mosque, and you said that you saw the ruins of that mosque. Did you see the very act of the destruction of the mosque?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: I didn't. I didn't dare leave my small hamlet. And this was during the night. No one dared move during the night. So you couldn't see anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know who destroyed it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: No one knows. These things happened at night. Just a powerful explosion was heard, and some people then said that the mosque had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I will go on to the event of August. Perhaps it would be best to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you mentioned in particular? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But let's go straight into private session. I think it's wiser. Thank you, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [redacted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please go ahead. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Believe me, my client and myself, we really feel with you and are sorry for what has happened.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: I believe you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you just a few questions. In your statement of the 16th of March, you said that it was -- the order was issued to hand in all the weapons to -- and to take it to Fajtovci.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: The military were in Fajtovci, as this territory came from Vugenovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Today you mentioned also the Crisis Staff in Fajtovci in connection with that weapons.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: The couriers came --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. One moment. Now, you speak, both of you, the same language. What you are saying needs to be translated into English and into French separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that speed and no interval between a question and the answer, the interpreters will never make it. So Mr. Trbojevic, I would kindly ask you to repeat your question. And you, sir, be kind enough to repeat your answer. Because like that we could not hear anything, and no one knows what was asked and what was answered. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Can we explain. Was the weapons to be handed into the Crisis Staff or the military in Fajtovci?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: In Fajtovci the crisis staff were the military, not civilians. That was not in Fajtovci. It was in Dosenovici between Fajtovci and Lukavica. Where their commander was and the military staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more question. Did you when carrying out the formalities for moving, did you sign a statement that your real estate, you are giving it to the municipality or the republic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: Yes. One could find these papers in the buildings and the attics.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: But are they translated and had been written in the land books?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: I don't know. I -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] You're repeating exactly the same mistake. Please pause --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're repeating the same mistake. Between the question and the answer, we require a pause. Not just we, but the interpreters mainly, first and foremost. So when he puts the question, sir, take your time before you start answering, because its needs to be translated to us. And the same applies to you, Mr. Trbojevic. As soon as he finishes with his -- with his answer, I mean, take a little bit of a pause before you proceed with the next question. Mind you, we do the same mistake when it's all in English. I mean, I can quite understand the problem that we cause to the interpreters when we do that now. I'm more aware of it now. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've asked the witness whether he knows whether that statement, where he leaves his real estate, whether that has been entered into the land books, the land register.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: I didn't check these books. I only know that I paid all my bills and the bills of my neighbours in order to be able to leave -- the neighbours who were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ask for the restitution?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT23
utterances.text: Well, I now live in the Federation, and it has been restituted to me. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Is there re-examination, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sir, your testimony -- your evidence has come to an end, thanks to the cooperation of the two Defence teams, you are in a position -- and also thanks to the short examination-in-chief of the Prosecution, you are in a position to return home today if you want to. In other words, you don't need to remain here in The Hague for the weekend and return here again on Monday. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, the other two Judges, myself, and the Tribunal in general, I would like to thank you for having come here to give evidence, and you will now be escorted out of the courtroom when all the curtains are down. We just want to make sure that your identity is kept undisclosed till the very end. And you will be looked after pending your return to where you would like to return. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, could you kindly escort the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So again once more, I thank Madam Fauveau and the Defence team because that helps smooth out things for everyone, I think, and it probably also spared the Tribunal a few hundred dollars, if not a few thousand dollars. I thank you. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if there's not been any change, it's my understanding we meet on Monday at 2.15 in Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And that brings me to what I was going to point out to you, that -- you recall that in April when we were having afternoon sittings, we had come to some kind of arrangement on the basis of which we had reduced the time of the sitting. The sitting time we kept to 3 hours 45 minutes, but we were finishing half an hour earlier or et cetera. I would be -- and I'm sure I haven't consulted the other two Judges, but I'm sure that we could repeat that, finish at 6.30 instead of 7.00 if that is okay with you. However, I would like you to sit down together, take some time, and it needs also to be referred then to the technical team and to the interpreters, because obviously if they say no, we won't be able to do it. But I think it would be in the interest of everyone to try and finish at 6.30 rather than 7.00 or even later. Again once more, I thank you. I wish you all a nice weekend, and we'll all meet again Monday in the afternoon. Thank you, Mr. Nicholls. Thank you, Mr. Cayley, for everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
